finding: A citation's `side` is agent-supplied (§6.1 schema row: "`side` is agent-supplied and defaults to `RIGHT`") and is load-bearing twice, but `cr` never derives or cross-checks it. (a) Grading: §6.2's `cited` row requires a citation that "lies outside the record's own unit", and §6.2.1 defines inside as path match plus line-in-hunk-range "on the same side". §3.4.4 makes a unit single-sided. So a citation pointing at a line INSIDE the record's own unit becomes `outside` merely by carrying `side: LEFT` — one agent-typed field converts `argued` into `cited`, and `cited` may assert. The guard that stops a record citing itself as evidence is bypassable by a field the record itself supplies. (b) Resolution: §6.2.3 resolves every citation "against the current head", unconditionally, while §6.1.2 correctly resolves anchors against the head for `RIGHT` and the merge base for `LEFT`. A legitimate `LEFT` citation about deleted code is therefore validated against head, where a same-numbered but unrelated line usually exists; it passes validation, gets a `content_hash` of text it does not describe, and §8.1.7 posts it to the author as `path:line`. Both an innocent and a deliberate path end with the assertion register bought and a posted pointer to code that does not support the claim. §6.2.2 shows the spec reasoned about side for probes ("a probe target is always RIGHT, so a record with a LEFT anchor can never reach `probed`") and §6.1.2 for anchors; only citations were left with side as free input. This is the same shape as the round-8 mutation-probe defect: an agent-typed field standing where a derived one belongs.
suggestion: Make `side` computed, not supplied: add it to §6.1.4's list of fields the agent MUST NOT write and reject a record that carries one. Have §6.2.3 resolve each citation against the head first and, only on failure, against the merge base, stamping `side` from whichever resolved; reject when neither does. Independently, harden §6.2.1's predicate so side cannot be the escape: a citation whose `path` and `line` fall inside the record's own unit on ANY side MUST count as inside. Keep the §6.2.2 sentence as the model — it is the correct treatment applied to probes.

finding: §4.4.4 requires that "a test-adequacy finding without a probe MUST be graded `argued` and therefore posted as a question", but §6.2.1 forbids `cr` from using anything except `citations` and the referenced probe to compute a grade: "The only inputs are `citations` and the referenced probe record". `axis` is not an input. Under §6.2 as written, a test-adequacy record that carries one citation outside its own unit — an existing test file, a helper, any line at all — is graded `cited`, may keep `kind: finding`, and §8.1.7 appends an evidence region listing that `path:line` as the assertion's support. The contradiction has a direction: an implementer coding §6.2.1 literally will post "this code is untested" as an assertion backed by a pointer. That is categorically the wrong instrument. A citation establishes that something EXISTS; a coverage finding asserts that something DOES NOT exist. No citation can establish an absence, so `cited` can never be the right register for a coverage claim, and §6.2.4's own caution ("never that it supports the summary") does not reach this because the grade has already licensed the assertion. §5.3 exists precisely because proving a test gap needs an experiment, and §4.4.3 only SHOULD-escalates to one.
suggestion: Resolve the contradiction explicitly rather than leaving two readings. Add `axis` (or a per-record `claim_polarity`) to §6.2.1's permitted grading inputs and state in §6.2: a record on the `test` axis, or any record whose summary asserts the absence of something, MUST be graded at most `argued` unless it references a supporting probe — citations cannot raise it. Then §4.4.4 becomes the statement of a rule §6.2 actually implements rather than prose §6.2.1 contradicts.

finding: §4.4.4 states "A test-adequacy finding without a probe MUST be graded `argued`", but §6.2.1 closes the grade inputs: "The only inputs are `citations` and the referenced probe record" — axis is not an input. §6.2's table grades a record `cited` whenever any resolved citation lies outside the record's own unit. A test-adequacy finding of the ordinary shape ("this branch has no test") that cites an existing or changed test file — which by construction sits outside the unit under review — is therefore graded `cited` by §6.2 and `argued` by §4.4.4. Two MUSTs in direct conflict, and an engineer implementing §6.2.1 literally produces exactly the outcome §4.4.4 exists to prevent: a coverage claim asserting in the finding register on the strength of a pointer to a file, with no experiment behind it.
suggestion: Pick one authority. Either delete §4.4.4's grading clause and let §6.2 be the sole grader (noting in §4.4 that a `test`-axis record reaches the assertion register only through a probe or a rule-origin citation), or add an explicit exception to §6.2.1 — e.g. "a record on the `test` axis MUST be graded `argued` unless it references a supporting probe; a citation alone never grades it `cited`" — and state it in the §6.2 table so the grader has one place to read.

finding: §4.5.1 makes a skipped role inactive — "A **role** is active when its axis is active, its `profiles` list is empty or names the resolved profile, and §4.6.4 did not report it skipped" — and §10.2.2 requires a complete row of cells only "for every active role". A skipped role therefore shrinks the set of cells completeness demands, and the round can be declared complete with a judgement lens that never ran. The honesty machinery does not reach it: §4.5.4, §10.1.3, §10.2's closing paragraph, and §11.1's always-printed list all speak of AXES only. Nothing in §10.1 or §10.2 has a slot for a skipped role, so `cr status` prints "complete" and names the disabled and unavailable axes while saying nothing about a lens that was skipped inside an active axis. §4.6.4's skip report happens at a different command at a different time, and is absent from §11.1's list, so `--quiet` may suppress it there too. The same hole swallows §4.3.1's half-axis case: it requires the reinvention half to "be marked unavailable per §4.5", but §4.5.4 discloses whole axes, so a half-unavailable axis has no reporting slot either. This directly contradicts P6 and VISION §2.7 ("Disabled axes are reported as disabled, never silently skipped") — the obligation was honoured at axis granularity and lost at role granularity, which is the granularity §10.2.2 actually counts. "Prerequisites" for a role is also undefined anywhere in the spec, which makes the escape hatch arbitrary in width.
suggestion: Extend §4.5.4 from axes to lenses: a disabled axis, an unavailable axis, an unavailable half-axis per §4.3.1, and a role skipped per §4.6.4 MUST each appear in the coverage report with its reason, and a complete verdict MUST be printed together with all of them. Add a corresponding line item to §10.1 (alongside §10.1.3) and add skipped roles and half-axes to §11.1's always-printed list. Define what a role's prerequisites are — the enumerable conditions of §4.3.1, §4.4.1, and §4.5.2 — so §4.6.4 cannot be satisfied by an arbitrary reason string.

finding: §5.3.5 asserts a guard it does not have: "`timeout`, `error`, `no-tests-selected`, and `inconclusive` MUST NOT support a `probed` grade, so neither an over-narrow filter, nor a runner whose output `cr` cannot parse, nor a run that never finished can manufacture evidence." The only filter failure those rungs catch is the EMPTY selection — §5.3.4 rung 4 fires when "the executed test count is known and equals zero". A filter that selects a non-empty set of tests which simply do not exercise the mutated line sails through: executed count > 0, failed count 0, rung 6 fires, result `no-test-failed`, and §5.2.2's filtered baseline passes on unmutated code because those same irrelevant tests were green. The record grades `probed`, keeps `kind: finding`, and posts as an assertion that the line is untested. The experiment actually performed shows only that the SELECTED tests do not cover the line — a proposition scoped by an agent-typed `--filter` that nothing relates to the mutated target. This is the residue of the round-8 defect on the one input that was left free: `target` is now derived from the patch, but the test set the conclusion is drawn over is still whatever the agent typed. The same shape applies to §5.4: `tests_failed >= 1` is attributed to the probe's own test, though `cr` never learns which test failed.
suggestion: Two changes. (1) Correct the prose: §5.3.5 should claim only what the ladder catches — that a filter selecting no tests cannot manufacture evidence — and state plainly that a filtered run scopes the conclusion to the selected tests. (2) Close the gap mechanically: require that a mutation probe support a `probed` grade only when its run was unfiltered, or when the filter's selected count equals the unfiltered baseline's `tests_run` (i.e. the filter narrowed nothing). Otherwise cap the record at `cited`/`argued`, or require §8.1.7's evidence region to state the assertion's scope explicitly as "the tests matching <filter>" rather than "the suite". For §5.4, record which tests failed when the runner's output permits, or state that attribution to the probe's test is assumed and not established.

finding: §5.4.5 says "A `passed` gap probe means only the test is missing" and lists only `timeout`, `error`, `no-tests-selected`, and `inconclusive` as results that "MUST NOT support a `probed` grade". By exclusion `passed` supports it, and §6.2's `probed` row confirms the grade comes from a probe "whose result supports the claim per §5.3 and §5.4". So a passing gap probe grades a record `probed` — the strongest register, exempt from §6.3's forcing, rendered by §8.1.7 as author-checkable proof — with NONE of the two guards §5.4.4 imposes on the `failed` branch: no baseline requirement and no requirement that the probe's subject relate to the finding. The run establishes one proposition: the behaviour under test is present at head. The record asserts a different one: no test in the existing suite covers it. The probe never executed the existing suite against that question, so the assertion is not the experiment's result. The only instrument in the spec that can prove a missing test is §5.3's mutation probe ("A mutation probe proves a test gap by breaking production code"), and §5.3.5 correctly restricts it to `no-test-failed` with a passing baseline. §5.4.5 hands the same register to a run that proved something else, and the code will faithfully implement it.
suggestion: Add `passed` to §5.4.5's non-supporting list: a `passed` gap probe MUST NOT support a `probed` grade. State the reason inline — it establishes the behaviour is present, not that the suite lacks a test, which only §5.3's `no-test-failed` can establish. A record left after a `passed` gap probe falls to `argued` under §6.2 and is posted as a question under §6.3, which is the honest register for "is this edge case covered anywhere?". Keep the at-most-`medium` severity cap. If a `probed` "missing test" claim is wanted, require the record to reference a §5.3 mutation probe instead.

finding: §6.1 now gives every citation a `side` (RIGHT default), but §6.2.3 and the `cited` row of the §6.2 table both say `cr` resolves citations "against the current head" unconditionally, with no LEFT branch — unlike §6.1.2, which explicitly resolves an anchor against the head for `side: RIGHT` and against the merge base for `side: LEFT`. A citation with `side: LEFT` names a deleted line, which by construction does not exist at the head. Two testers write opposite tests: one asserts that `cr record` rejects every LEFT citation with exit code 1 (path gone or line out of range), the other asserts it resolves against the merge base and accepts. The consequence is not cosmetic — §6.2.3 rejects the whole record, so under the first reading a record about deleted code can never carry a citation, can never be graded `cited`, and any merge file containing one fails outright; the `side` field on the citation object and §6.2.1's "on the same side" inside/outside test would then be dead weight. `content_hash`, which `cr` computes at record time, has the same unstated reference point.
suggestion: Mirror §6.1.2 in §6.2.3 and in the `cited` table row: `cr` MUST resolve a citation with `side: RIGHT` against the current head and one with `side: LEFT` against the merge base, and MUST compute `content_hash` against the same reference. State the exit-1 rejection per side.

finding: The default for `tests.probe_path_template` is `<root of the first `tests.globs` entry>/cr_probe_<probe-id><ext>`, and `<ext>` appears nowhere else in the spec. Nothing says whether it is the extension of the `--test` file the agent supplied to §5.4.2, or an extension derived from the first `tests.globs` entry (and if so, whether `*Test.php` yields `.php` or `Test.php`). A tester cannot assert the resulting path for any profile that omits the field. It also collides with §5.1.6: the leftover-artefact scan globs the template with only the `<probe-id>` position replaced by `*`, so a template that still carries a literal `<ext>` matches no real file on disk and the cleanliness check silently never fires.
suggestion: Define `<ext>` explicitly (e.g. "the file extension of the test file supplied to `cr probe run --kind gap`, including the dot"), and state in §5.1.6 that the artefact glob is computed after every placeholder except `<probe-id>` has been substituted.

finding: §3.6.6 calls a note "unverified hearsay" and makes it revocable, but defers every consequence of revocation past the point where the damage is done: "any coverage cell or record citing a retracted note MUST be reported as needing re-evaluation in the next round rather than silently retained". Within the current round the record is retained with no report, and nothing in §7.1, §7.2, §8.1, or §8.5 drops or re-grades it. So a reviewer who retracts a note mid-round — precisely because they learned it was wrong — can still have `cr draft` and `cr post --confirm` send the assertion built on it. Because v0.1 ends at posting (§1.3.6, §9), "the next round" may never arrive for this pull request, which makes the deferral unbounded in practice. Two further inconsistencies follow. §8.1.6 requires the posted provenance region to name "the note and its source per §3.6.3" for a record resting on a `source: note` claim — for a retracted note the spec does not say whether the region reads a removed entry, names a dangling id, or is omitted. And §3.3.2 admits such a claim "rests on weaker provenance", which is the whole reason §8.1.6 discloses it; retraction is the reviewer stating that the weak provenance failed, and it should carry more weight than a next-round note, not less.
suggestion: Make retraction take effect in the round it happens. Require that on `cr note --remove`, every current-round record or cell citing that note be re-evaluated immediately: the record MUST be forced to `kind: question` (or blocked from drafting) and the retraction MUST be reported by `cr status` and in the round summary, in addition to the next-round report §3.6.6 already requires. State what §8.1.6's provenance region does for a retracted note — the honest answer is that the record no longer has provenance to disclose and so no longer qualifies for the assertion register. Keep the retention of the record itself so the decision stays auditable.

finding: §4.1.7 makes `intent-gaps.ndjson` a pure derivation: "On each successful `cr map record`, `cr` MUST derive `intent-gaps.ndjson` mechanically as the claims of the current round mapped to zero units." §4.1.8 then stamps `set_aside_note` onto a gap entry, and §10.2.3 makes that stamp the only thing that unblocks completeness for an unimplemented claim. Nothing says what happens to the stamp when the mapping is re-recorded — and §4.1.6 explicitly permits that, since `cr map record` "MUST replace `mapping.ndjson` for the current round". A literal re-derivation silently discards every set-aside decision the reviewer already made, re-blocking §10.2.3 with no report; a merge-preserving derivation is a different implementation with different failure modes. Neither is specified.
suggestion: State the carry-forward rule in §4.1.7: re-derivation MUST preserve `set_aside_note` for any claim that is still unmapped, and MUST drop the stamp — reporting that it did — for a claim that has since become mapped. Add the surviving-stamp count to what `cr status` reports per §10.1.2 so the preservation is observable rather than assumed.

finding: §4.6.5 gates the non-intent axes on whether "a mapping exists for the current round and head", but the only observable is `mapping.ndjson`, whose records carry `round` and `head` per §2.3.3 and which §9.3.4 clears on a new round. A legitimately empty mapping — every unit mapped to zero claims, which happens whenever an issue key resolves but the agent extracts no claims, so the intent axis is available per §4.5.3 but there is nothing to map — is byte-identical to a cleared or never-written file. Two testers write contradictory tests: one asserts `cr map record` with an empty file unblocks the remaining axes, the other asserts `cr review` still exits 4. Under the second reading the pull request deadlocks permanently, since §4.6.6's escape hatch only covers an unavailable intent axis.
suggestion: Make the gate a recorded fact rather than an inference from record count: have `cr map record` stamp the round and head of the stored mapping on `meta.json`, and have §4.6.5 read that stamp, so an empty mapping is distinguishable from an absent one.

finding: §6.1's citation object now carries `side`, and §6.2.1's inside/outside predicate compares hunk ranges "on the same side", so a `side: LEFT` citation is legal. But §6.2.3 resolves every citation entry unconditionally "against the current head", contradicting §6.1.2, which fixes the resolution base per side — head for `RIGHT`, merge base for `LEFT`. A LEFT citation is therefore range-checked against the wrong file version, and §8.1.7 compounds it by rendering every stored citation into the posted evidence region as bare `path:line` with no side, so the author looks up a merge-base line number in the head file and sees unrelated code. That is a wrong assertion reaching the author with no way to tell it is wrong.
suggestion: Make §6.2.3 side-aware: resolve a citation against the head when `side` is `RIGHT` and against the merge base when it is `LEFT`, mirroring §6.1.2's wording, and reject an out-of-range line against that base. Then require §8.1.7 to render a `LEFT` citation with its side made explicit (or forbid `side: LEFT` on citations outright, as §6.2.2 already does for probe targets, and drop `side` back to a constant).

finding: §6.1 now gives every citation a `side` (agent-supplied, default `RIGHT`), and §6.2.1 uses that side to decide inside/outside a unit. But §6.2.3 still resolves *every* citation "against the current head" and rejects with exit code 1 an entry "whose path does not exist or whose line is out of range", with no side branch. §6.1.2 and §9.2.1 explicitly support records about deleted code via `side: LEFT` anchors. A `LEFT` citation names a line in the merge base — possibly in a file the PR deleted outright — so validating it against head either rejects a legitimate deletion finding outright or silently validates the wrong line, and `content_hash` (also computed at record time by §6.2.3) is then hashed from head content that has nothing to do with the cited line.
suggestion: Mirror §6.1.2 in §6.2.3: resolve a citation with `side: RIGHT` against the current head and one with `side: LEFT` against the merge base, and hash `content_hash` from the same side. Amend the `cited` row of the §6.2 grade table to say "resolved against the head for `side: RIGHT` and the merge base for `side: LEFT`" rather than "against the current head".

finding: §8.1.7 promises that the strongest register is checkable — for `probed` it carries "the probe's `kind`, `target`, `filter`, `result`, and `output_tail`, so the strongest register is the one the author can check rather than the one they must take on trust". It omits the one artefact that makes it checkable: `input`, the patch or test file `cr` actually executed (§5.5). For a mutation probe the author sees "target line 42, result no-test-failed" but not what was changed at line 42, so a semantically inert mutation — a comment, a whitespace edit, a log string, dead code — produces a genuine `no-test-failed` against a passing baseline, grades `probed`, and posts as "this line is untested" with nothing the author can inspect to catch it. `cr` cannot judge whether a mutation changed behaviour (invariant 1, P5), which is exactly why the check has to be delegated to the author, and exactly what §8.1.7 already claims to do. For a gap probe it is worse: §5.4.4 concedes that a `failed` result means "either the behaviour is wrong or the supplied test is wrong, and `cr` cannot distinguish the two", yet the region shows the failure output without the test that produced it, leaving the author the one distinction `cr` admits it cannot make and no material to make it with.
suggestion: Add `input` to §8.1.7's list for both probe kinds, so the executed patch or test file is rendered inside the `cr`-owned evidence region. Cap it — reuse `tests.output_tail_bytes` or add `post.max_probe_input_bytes` — and state that when the input is truncated the region MUST say so. If the volume cost under §1.6 is judged too high for gap tests, at minimum require the mutation patch verbatim (it is one hunk) and drop the sentence claiming checkability for the case where the artefact is withheld.

finding: §2.6.1.6 mandates that "every hit, record, and dismissal" be appended to `rule-stats.ndjson`, but no command in §11 is named as the producer of a `dismissal` event and nothing observes the agent's confirmation that §2.6.1.5 requires — an unconfirmed hit is simply "dropped", leaving no observable moment at which a dismissal is written. The file also has no idempotency key, unlike its sibling `triage.ndjson`, whose §7.3.1 keys events by `(PR, round, record id, action)` precisely so re-running a command cannot inflate counts. Detection is run by both `cr rules check` (§11) and `cr review` (§4.6.1 carries rule hits into prompts), so the same `(rule, path, line, round, head)` hit is appended more than once in an ordinary loop, inflating §2.6.3.4's dead-rule window and §7.3.2's per-rule statistics.
suggestion: Name the producing command and derivation for `dismissal` (e.g. `cr record` writes one per current-round hit that no recorded record cites), and give §2.6.1.6 the same idempotency rule as §7.3.1: events keyed by `(rule id, path, line, round, head, event type)` and overwritten rather than appended on re-run.

finding: §5.3.4 and §5.4.3 each declare that the probe's result "MUST be determined by the first matching rung of this ladder, which is total over every run". §5.1.7 then says a probe whose post-run cleanliness check fails "MUST be recorded with result `error`" — a determination made after the ladder has already produced a result, and one no rung can express. Combined with §5.5.1 ("Probe records MUST be immutable once written") the write order is unspecified: it is not stated whether the cleanliness check runs before the record is written (so `error` is the only value ever persisted) or after (so an immutable record must be amended, which §5.5.1 forbids).
suggestion: State in §5.1.7 that the cleanliness check runs before the probe record is written and overrides the ladder outcome, and soften the totality claims in §5.3.4 and §5.4.3 to "total over every run that leaves the sandbox clean per §5.1.6".

finding: The two probe ladders disagree on abnormal termination. §5.3.4 rung 3 fires on "the runner could not be started, **or exited on a signal**"; §5.4.3 rung 2 fires only on "the runner could not be started". A gap probe whose runner is killed by a signal (OOM, SIGSEGV) after emitting partial output that `tests.count_pattern` still matches therefore falls through to rung 6 and is recorded `failed` — and §5.4.4 makes a supported `failed` gap probe carry severity at least `high`. A crashed process becomes high-severity evidence, which is exactly the direction §5.3.4 rung 3 was written to prevent.
suggestion: Add "or exited on a signal" to §5.4.3 rung 2, so both ladders classify abnormal termination as `error` before any count-based rung is consulted.

finding: §5.6.4 says `probe.max_per_round` "MUST cap probe executions per round; the cap being hit MUST be reported, never silently applied", without saying what the invocation past the cap does. §1.6.2 pins the comparable comment cap to a block with exit code 1; here a tester cannot tell whether the eleventh `cr probe run` refuses (and with which exit code), or runs after printing a notice — "never silently applied" reads either way.
suggestion: Pin it as §1.6.2 does: the run past the cap MUST be refused with a named exit code and the count reported.

finding: §7.1.5 requires `cr` to write, alongside each record's agent region, "the normalised hash of those regions concatenated in marker order", and calls it "the only observable basis for detecting a user edit". That aggregate hash has no consumer and cannot acquire one. §7.1.6 needs per-record content, not an aggregate — it preserves "bodies for records whose body differs from `rendered.json`". The one use its own sentence invites, detecting whether the human touched the draft, is forbidden by §8.5.4: "`cr` MUST NOT report whether `draft.md` changed as evidence of human involvement". And §8.1.2 guarantees the agent rewrites every body in `render.lang` before the human ever opens the file, so the aggregate is certain to differ on every round — it is a signal whose value is constant. It costs an implementation, a test, and a line of state, buys nothing, and its framing tempts exactly the human-involvement inference §8.5.4 rules out.
suggestion: Drop the concatenated hash from §7.1.5 and keep the per-record agent regions, which §7.1.6 genuinely uses. Replace the sentence "This is the only observable basis for detecting a user edit" with a statement of what the file is actually for: preserving edited bodies across regeneration per §7.1.6, and nothing else, since §8.5.4 forbids treating a draft change as evidence that a human read it.

finding: §8.1.6 requires the provenance region when the record "takes its grade from a citation with `origin: rule`". When a record carries both a rule citation and an agent citation lying outside its unit, either alone earns `cited` under §6.2, so whether the grade is "taken from" the rule citation has two defensible readings and two contradictory tests on whether the posted comment carries a provenance block.
suggestion: Restate the trigger mechanically: emit the provenance region whenever any stored citation carries `origin: rule`, regardless of what else qualifies the record for `cited`.
